https://www.politico.eu/article/pope-leo.text: PARIS — Pope Leo XIV urged France to embrace dialogue and diversity Friday, in a veiled swipe at populists as he arrived in Paris for a four-day visit. His appeal came seven months before France’s presidential election, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen leading opinion polls for the National Rally and traditional parties struggling to hold voters after nearly a decade of Emmanuel Macron’s presidency. “A truly free society” prevents “authoritarian tendencies,” the pope said in a speech delivered alongside President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace. Advertisement Advertisement The pope named no politician or party. But his defense of diversity and religious freedom lands as Le Pen’s National Rally campaigns against immigration ahead of a presidential election she hopes to win for the first time. “This dialogue is all the more urgent in the context of present-day France, where the people of differing cultural and religious backgrounds are called to live together,” the pontiff continued. Standing in front of French government members and church dignitaries, the pope also argued against pushing religion out of public life, weeks after the National Rally said it was in favor of banning the Muslim headscarf. “Righteous secularism doesn’t mean excluding religion from public spaces,” he said. Macron said the pope brought “hope” to France and praised his work on artificial intelligence and human dignity. The papal visit will take Leo from the Élysée to UNESCO, Notre-Dame Cathedral and a youth vigil at the Stade de France. He will celebrate Mass on Saturday, expected to gather 600,000 people on the Champs-Elysées in Paris. French politics have become deeply polarized in recent years, with the far-right National Rally and the far-left France Unbowed gaining popularity, just as traditional parties struggle to attract voters after a decade of Macron’s presidency. Advertisement Advertisement According to Antonio Spadaro, undersecretary of the Vatican’s Dicastery for Culture and Education, the pontiff will not offer voting instructions while in France nor criticize those who want to vote for Le Pen. Those attracted to nationalism, he said, often have legitimate concerns about identity and “the fear of losing it” but have been “offered the wrong answer.” “The pope will not tell the French to be less French,” said Spadaro in an interview with POLITICO ahead of the visit. “Roots are a good thing. The trouble begins when roots are used as walls.”

Photograph: PR HANDOUT View image in fullscreen The baby, from the Ipswich area west of Brisbane, died almost a week after being taken to hospital with ‘significant internal injuries’. Photograph: PR HANDOUT Queensland Queensland man charged with murder after three-month-old son dies from ‘significant internal injuries’ Uneeb Ullah, 28, from Ipswich, has been remanded in custody after his arrest on Tuesday evening for the alleged murder of the child Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Ben Smee Wed 7 Oct 2026 01.39 EDT Last modified on Wed 7 Oct 2026 04.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Queensland man has been charged with the murder of his three-month-old baby son, after the boy died in hospital this week. The infant, from the Ipswich area west of Brisbane, died almost a week after being taken to hospital with “significant internal injuries”. The boy had been on life support. Uneeb Ullah, 28, was arrested on Tuesday evening and charged with the boy’s murder, which is designated a domestic violence offence. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email His matter was mentioned briefly in court on Wednesday but Ullah was not required to appear and did not enter a plea. Police said detectives from the Child Protection Investigation Unit launched an investigation on 1 October after the boy was taken to Ipswich hospital with significant injuries, and that the nature of those injuries prompted hospital staff to report the matter to police. He was later transferred to the Queensland children’s hospital. View image in fullscreen Police arrested Ullah on Tuesday evening. Photograph: PR HANDOUT Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, DI Michael Manago said the mother of the child was “extremely upset” and that both parents, who were born overseas, have limited support. The boy was the couple’s only child. “This is a terribly tragic event involving a very vulnerable young member of the community,” Det Insp. Manago said. “The boy’s mother is extremely upset as you can imagine; this is a terribly tragic event. “She is struggling, but we’re offering her all the support that we can through this very difficult time.” Police said they had spoken to the couple several times since they opened the investigation. The investigation would include looking at the “nature and dynamics” of the boy’s parents’ relationship. “It’s an incredibly confronting and difficult investigation,” Manago said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “We were conducting our investigation throughout the last number of days and gathering evidence. When Ullah’s case came before the court on Wednesday, police prosecutor Ben Messina asked it be stood down until later in the day. “I received a phone call this morning … that potentially more material would be provided and asked [that] this matter be stood down to the end of the list,” Messina said of the “relatively vague request”. The magistrate agreed to re-mention the case if other charges were laid. Kirstyn Nicholson, a Legal Aid solicitor representing Ullah, did not apply for bail and sought an adjournment. Ullah was remanded in custody until the matter returns to court on 26 October. – With AAP This story was amended on 7 October 2026. https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-millions-i.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PRqV Prefer DW on Google Former Hungarian Development Minister Miklos Sesztak is suspected of accepting millions in bribes during Viktor Orban's rule [FILE: July 30, 2017] Image: Robert Szaniszlo/ZUMA/IMAGO Advertisement Hungarian authorities have recovered nearly $20 million (€17.7 million) in hidden cash during a corruption investigation into a former minister under ex-Prime Minister Viktor Orban . The country's newly established National Asset Recovery and Protection Office said Friday that investigators discovered the money during searches linked to former National Development Minister Miklos Sesztak. The discovery is part of a sweeping anti-corruption campaign launched by Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who defeated Orban in April's parliamentary election. Where did Hungarian investigators find the hidden cash? The money was discovered during two days of searches in the capital, Budapest, and three Hungarian counties. Investigators found large quantities of cash buried in forests, concealed in agricultural buildings, warehouses and residential properties, as well as stored in an expensive safe at a secluded location. The recovered money included 5.07 billion Hungarian forints (€13.3 million, $15.3 million), €2.66 million (€2.9 million) and $1.26 million (€1.08 million). According to Finance Minister Andras Karman, 12 employees of the Hungarian State Treasury spent eight hours counting the banknotes using five counting machines. The agency also released a video showing investigators kneeling beside large piles of bundled cash and digging into the ground in what appeared to be a forest at night. Authorities said the seized money had been deposited into an account belonging to the Hungarian state treasury. What corruption allegations does former minister Sesztak face? Sesztak served as Orban's national development minister between 2014 and 2018. He is suspected of accepting more than $37 million (€33 million) in bribes and kickbacks connected to the purchase of overpriced used buses by state-owned transport companies and state construction projects. The former minister was taken into police custody in late September. He has denied wrongdoing. His lawyer, Gabor Papp, so far did not respond to a request for comment on the latest discovery. How has Hungary's Prime Minister Magyar reacted? Magyar described the recovered cash as a turning point in his government's efforts to tackle alleged corruption under Orban. The discovery "officially marks the end of the Fidesz-KDNP mafia," he wrote on Facebook, referring to Orban's former governing coalition. "As of today, Viktor Orbán is a proven mafia boss. A fallen mafia boss. And Fidesz is a criminal organization," Magyar added. Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar has launched a sweeping anti-corruption campaign targeting alleged abuses under his predecessor Viktor Orban [FILE: November 10, 2026] Image: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS Magyar's center-right, pro-European Tisza party won a landslide victory in April, ending Orban's 16-year rule. The new prime minister has pledged to repair Hungary 's relations with the European Union , which had been strained by years of disputes under Orban. His government established the anti-corruption agency with investigative and prosecutorial powers to pursue suspected corruption and misuse of public funds. Who else is being investigated in Hungary's corruption crackdown? Magyar has dubbed the campaign "Operation Purgatory." Several other senior figures from Orban's time in office have been detained as part of separate investigations. Among them is former central bank governor and economy minister Gyorgy Matolcsy, once considered one of Orban's closest allies. Matolcsy is being investigated over the alleged misuse of a central bank foundation that received 288 billion forints ($818 million, €787 million) in public assets. He and other former officials under investigation have denied wrongdoing. Police also detained Orban's younger brother earlier this week as part of an investigation into suspected human trafficking and influence peddling. Viktor Orban's younger brother was detained as part of an investigation into suspected human trafficking and influence peddling [FILE: November 9, 2026] Image: Viktor Veres/HVG/dpa/picture alliance Orban has condemned the investigations as political "tyranny" aimed at removing him from Hungary's political landscape. He has described his brother's detention as an act of political revenge. According to a survey by pollster Median published by news website HVG this week, 70% of respondents considered the anti-corruption campaign "very important." A separate Median survey showed support for Orban's Fidesz party had fallen to 16% of voters by November, roughly half its level before the April election.
